title: A Transformer-Derived Iterative Preconditioner
claim: A trained transformer's internal weights show a simple recurring structure that progressively improves conditioning of its input across layers.
layout: 2 panels: left heatmap grid (2 rows by 5 layers), right line plot
description: The figure has two parts. On the left is a 2x5 grid of small square heatmaps showing learned weight products. The top row is W_QK and the bottom row is VP, and the columns are Layers 2, 8, 14, 20 and 26. Each heatmap uses a red-white-blue diverging colormap. Almost all of them show a strong, clean diagonal and faint off-diagonal noise, which points to a simple two-scalar structure. The diagonal's sign and magnitude change from layer to layer. Two colorbars sit to the right of the grid, one for each row. On the right is a line plot of log10 condition number of X^T X against layer, from 0 to 30. A dark median line with dots falls from about 3.4 to about 0.8. A gray band marks the middle 80% of the data. The band widens sharply near the last layers. The eye goes first to the saturated diagonals and then to the falling curve.
caption: Extracting a conditioning primitive. Left: Representative learned weight products WQK,ℓ and WV P,ℓ, showing the dominant two-scalar structure in Eq. (3). Right: Median condition number of the context Gram matrix across layers of the trained transformer, decreasing from roughly 3,000 to below 10 at the best layer.
abstract: Transformers trained on in-context prediction problems can learn known numerical algorithms, e.g., gradient descent. We go further, showing that their internal computations can reveal new algorithms with provable guarantees. A softmax-attention transformer trained to solve linear systems $Xw=y$ implicitly improves matrix conditioning. Tracing $XX^\top$ reveals an iterative preconditioning primitive, which we develop into RAPID, a standalone algorithm requiring no learned components. RAPID is an anytime preconditioner for symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices, using randomized mixing and sparse local corrections to improve conditioning. Proof-of-concept experiments on synthetic and real-world problems consistently improve conditioning and reduce conjugate gradient iterations needed to reach a target accuracy. For a Haar-mixing idealization, we prove convergence to any fixed target condition number regardless of spectral distribution, with only logarithmic dependence on initial conditioning. Together, these results show how a transformer can discover a broadly applicable numerical algorithm.
